UNIT AMBIGUITY, deliberate. Two levels: the averia is a compulsory ad valorem levy pooling the cost of convoy protection across all shippers; the asiento is the contracted vehicle administering it, whose participes pool capital and share loss proportionally. Coded 1 for the vehicle. If the levy is the intended unit the coding still holds, but the members differ.

THE CELL THAT MATTERS, and the project's own note flags it as open. The pooled object is protection, and the hazard is an adversary who responds to the defence mounted rather than a storm - which makes losses correlated across participants and the pooling synchronising rather than diversifying. Bears directly on why the pool failed. Vault note 'The asiento de averia is the pooling-to-corporation hinge' says where this sits on the determinate-contingent typology is better asked than assumed; coded low on that authority.

INVERTS THE VOC PATTERN. There is no subscribed permanent capital: contributions were called as needed and non-payment forfeited the share. Capital is therefore immobile in the sense that it cannot be withdrawn, but it was never locked in as a fixed sum either. The mills accumulate capital by call, the joint-stock company by subscription - a genuine structural difference, and the one Harris gestures at with the cost-book analogy.

DECIDES THE HARRIS DISPUTE ON THE STRUCTURAL QUESTION. Pariers were free to sell their rights WITHOUT THE CONSENT of the other pariers, and the 1182 Castel enfeoffment schedules the tax on transactions in halves, thirds and quarters - so fractional alienation was routine and fiscally anticipated by the twelfth century. Harris does not deny transferability; he requires an impersonal exchange, which is a property of the venue, not of the share.

the equality rule made shares identical irrespective of holder, which Le Bris, Goetzmann & Pouget call 'a preliminary for depersonalization' - their hedge, preserved here. Contrast the societas, where the share was tied to a specific partner. Coded P rather than 1 because the authors themselves stop short.
inferred from universitas doctrine and from forfeiture as the sanction for non-payment; not evidenced directly

a single jointly-owned asset, not mutualisation of members' idiosyncratic risks. NB the milling pariages did contract mutual insurance BETWEEN themselves - pooling at the inter-firm level, not within the firm, and a candidate for separate coding.
inapplicable: LR4 is 0

TWO SOURCES AT ONCE, and the tension is the point. The mills were held by comital enfeoffment (Bazacle 1177 and 1184, Castel 1182), a feudal grant; but their legal personality came from the ius commune without any approbation. Neither state-charter nor purely customary. The vocabulary cannot currently express authorization from received learned law - a candidate defect, flagged not fixed.

THE CELL WHERE HARRIS AND LE BRIS/GOETZMANN/POUGET ACTUALLY DISAGREE. Harris reads the mills as providing services to the community and distributing accumulated profits, which is mutual-provision; the others read a profit-seeking firm, which is commercial-profit. Coded mixed to hold the dispute open rather than resolve it by fiat. Resolving this cell resolves much of the debate.

HALF-PRESENT, and the whole point of the form. D'Amico: household names 'did not need to correspond with any given individual, possessing a kind of legal personality'. A kind of — de facto and unbounded by any grant. No charter, no incorporation, no juridical act. Contrast joint_stock and the waqf, where personality is conferred or doctrinally constituted. This is the cell on which the five-component framework is tested from outside the Roman-law lineage.

Fictive households held assets and acted in their own names — 'investing, buying, selling, borrowing, and lending as independent legal entities'. Nakai Iwanosuke 'founded' the Osaka store in 1806 aged five and died in 1807; the nonexistent Iwanosuke went on paying interest on the main house's prospective funds, over 20,000 ryō between 1806 and 1845.

Not recorded, and D'Amico says why: partnership accounts were designated nakama-goto and non-adjudicable, 'so few legal sources survive', and 'how liability worked in the case of bankruptcy for fictive household entities remains a mystery'. Whether a fictive household could sue in its own name is unanswerable from this source. NOT coded 0 — the silence is evidentiary, not substantive.

Assets divided among entities across shogunal, suzerain and some 260 domain jurisdictions, exploiting the cost of collecting a debt across a border. 'Nakai Shinsaburō in Sendai, as a separate household from Nakai Genzaemon in Hino, did not bear responsibility for the latter's debts — or vice versa.' Partition is jurisdictional rather than juridical.
No evidence on whether a partner could force liquidation or withdraw capital at will. The Karasu dissolution of 1839 shows dissolution happening, not the right to compel it.

OBSERVED ABSENCE. In the 1839 failure of Ōta-ya Uhe, the sake brewery at Karasu, the three partners' debt was 'held under their three individual names, not the fictive name of the store' and divided equally despite uneven shares; one partner sold his house and belongings to repay. Owners were not shielded. Coded medium on one case, and D'Amico himself calls bankruptcy liability a mystery.

'A clear separation existed between household and business accounts, leaving no overlap between the expenditures of Nakai family members and the accounting at each store.' But AP4 is written around a founder and a corpus — a waqf-shaped category, already flagged in this vocabulary — and an ie that is inherited generation after generation does not have a founder's estate in that sense. Coded P at low confidence with the comparative-concept caveat live.

Ōtō Osamu's definition, quoted: an ie is 'an organizational entity that seeks to exist eternally, that bears a specific house name, house assets, and house line of business, and that is inherited generation after generation'. In 1834 the fourth Nakai Genzaemon inherited the Sendai store's name; the manager submitted the succession document and signed Shinsaburō's name himself — 'because (the new) Shinsaburō is not present, matters have been entrusted to me, the store manager, in his stead'. Succession by proxy, for a person who need not exist.
'The household, much like a corporation, waqf, or entail, was eternal.' Not a venture with a term.
Revocability not addressed.
Mutability of purpose not addressed. The ie definition names a 'house line of business' (kagyō) which would bear on this, but D'Amico does not pursue it.

Each store held its own name, capital and books — the feature D'Amico uses to draw the Medici comparison, where 'each office underneath the Medici main house existed as a separate legal entity, each a partnership with its own name, capital, and books'.

Profits after interest 'remained in store coffers', so capital was retained rather than distributed. But lock-in was not binding on the main house: in 1782 the Nakai unilaterally converted the four Sendai outside partners' investment into interest-only, stopping profit distribution. Locked in against the partners, not against the principal.

THE DECISIVE CELL, and D'Amico states it flatly: Tokugawa merchant houses 'failed to develop joint-stock equity finance or transferability in the absence of any real use for these features'. Shares (kuchi) existed and were proportioned — Sōma 1783 divided nineteen shares, nine to the main house, ten to Nakai Shinsaburō, one reserved to the manager — but they did not circulate. Perpetuity and partition without transferable claims.

Follows CI3. Shares are held by named partners in named proportions; nothing is depersonalised. Contrast bazacle_mill CI3=1/CI4, where alienation without co-owner consent is attested from the twelfth century.

From the Karasu case alone: debt held under the partners' individual names and 'divided equally' despite an uneven split in shares, which is joint rather than several. One observation, and D'Amico calls the general question a mystery. Low confidence and it should not carry a comparative claim.
Partners bore losses on their own estates in the one documented failure. No veil operated at the point it would have mattered.

'Profits and losses split in accordance with the distribution of shares among the investing partners.' The Sōma agreement of 1783 is explicit on the loss side: the manager's single share was '…to be used as a bonus for hard work; however, losses will be divided by 19 shares.'
Capital pooled across partners and across stores; D'Amico cites Uemura, 'Ōmi shōnin no keiei to kiken bunsan' — Ōmi merchant management and risk dispersion — as the literature on the practice.

Stores spread across Sendai, Osaka, Kyoto, Edo, Sōma, Ishinomaki, Onomichi, Ōtawara, Nagoya and elsewhere, and across trade lines. Decorrelating rather than synchronising — the Fugger contrast, where activity was diversified but the counterparty was not. Whether the Nakai concentrated a counterparty is not addressed here and is the obvious follow-up.

The Sōma clause divides losses by nineteen shares including the manager's bonus share, which reads as symmetric exposure. Coded low: the clause is terse and could equally mean the manager's share is excluded from the loss base. Verify against Egashira.
Entitlement follows the partnership agreement and the prospective-fund investment, not membership in a body or beneficiary status.

A store rule, quoted: 'Regarding all store affairs, no matter how insignificant, the main members [of the store] should gather and without reservation share their opinions, deliberate, and decide on the issue at hand.' D'Amico adds that all major decisions including the appointment of managers involved senior staff in consultation with the head, 'who could not make unilateral decisions'. Collective governance inside a form with no legal personality.

Inapplicable: MG1=contract, so there is no membership whose entry could be restricted. Entitlement runs through the partnership agreement and the prospective-fund investment. Recruitment data exist — 43 per cent of hires between 1836 and 1862 came from outside the Nakai's home province of Ōmi, against houses where over 90 per cent shared a common origin — but employment is not entry to the entity, and coding it here would answer a different question.

THE CELL THAT MAKES THIS A COUNTER-CASE. No charter, no grant, no authorising act. The samurai authorities enforced private contracts and distinguished kane kuji from hon kuji, but 'flatly refused to handle cases related to the settlement of accounts in partnerships, explicitly designating them as one of the primary categories of non-adjudicable issues (nakama-goto)'. The law offered no tool for forming a business. These entities arose against a standing refusal, not merely in its absence.
Trading and brewing enterprises across some forty stores. No pious or mutual-provision limb.
No monopoly franchise attaches to the entity. Contrast kabu_nakama and the alleenrecht, where the privilege is the asset.

THE DEFINITIONAL CELL. The fictive household is an identity wrapper in the strict sense: a name that looks like a person, holds assets, signs documents and is registered, with no body behind it. Yamahiroya-Chōbe of 1870 is the limiting case — 'a store name recognized as a member of the neighborhood (chō) without a flesh-and-blood head in existence'.

Registered and legible to the state precisely as a household. A store clerk placed the five-year-old Iwanosuke's seal on the teraokuri shōmon in 1806; clerks cited his youth on the 1827 shūmon aratame-chō and, after he died in 1807, switched the excuse to sickness in 1829 and 1835. The register recorded a household that did not exist. Legibility achieved without the state ever conferring entity status.

Outside partners at Sendai were explicitly passive — 'the four together served as passive partners' — while non-kin professional managers ran the stores. But managers could hold shares, so the capital-labour line is not clean.

Applicable because CF1 is P. The Sōma manager's share appears in the loss base ('losses will be divided by 19 shares'), so the agent bears some capital loss — but see LR6, where the same clause is ambiguous. Low, and dependent on the same verification.

Multiple principals throughout: Nishikawa Denji formed 1741-57 by twenty-one investors holding forty shares; Sōma 1783 founded by the main house together with Nakai Shinsaburō, itself a fictive household. Fictive households could become founding partners in further fictive households — entities compounding, not merely persons.

The defining arrangement: an investor entrusts capital to an agent who trades and lends it, then repays principal and a share of profits. Peng Daya, verbatim: 從韃主至僞太子僞公主皆付回回以銀 — from the Mongol emperor down to the princes and princesses, all entrust their silver to the Hui-hui. Coded 1 rather than P despite the Fakhr al-Din case where the ortoq added his own capital; see the note on CF3.

Corroborated by Rashid al-Din 725, where investors could do nothing when partners lost capital and 'tried hard to compensate their ortoqs'. Downgraded from high to medium because the step from that instance to the form is inside the paragraph governed by 'it can be hypothesized'. The Fakhr al-Din leg of it rests on Vassaf's SILENCE about the Tibi family's obligations. Confidence downgraded accordingly; .NR is a defensible alternative if the maintainer judges the hypothesis too thin.

THE SOURCE SAYS IT IS UNKNOWN, IN TERMS: 'The maximum time of validity of a Mongol-ortoq partnership is not entirely clear.' Both readings are attested and neither is dominant — Nicolo and Maffeo Polo were free to leave the Golden Horde once they had sold the wares entrusted by Berke, and maritime merchants were contracted for a single voyage, but 'some trusted and experienced ortoqs might have been continuously employed by their Mongol investors, since the duration of these partnerships was at the will of the partners.' Do NOT import single-venture from commenda; that is the inference this row exists to refuse.

Capital is entrusted per venture and per investor rather than held as a common fund; an ortoq holding several partnerships at once held them separately. Medium — Enkhbold nowhere describes the accounting, and this is read off the contracting pattern.

The claim arises from the entrustment, not from membership in a body. The term ortoq designates a merchant standing in a personal gift-exchange relationship with a high-status Mongol or funded by the Mongol government.

ENDICOTT-WEST 1989 IS THE SOURCE THAT WOULD FILL THIS AND SHE IS NOT IN HAND. Enkhbold shows ortoqs carrying paiza and jarliq and drawing on the jam relay system, which is a grant of privilege by the ruler, but says nothing about what authorised the partnership itself. Private contract, customary practice and state charter are all live and the source does not choose.
Trade and money-lending for gain throughout; no charitable or mutual-provision purpose anywhere in the record.

The paiza is the wrapper: an ortoq carrying one could exact provisions and mounts from the relay stations, and Enkhbold notes that restricting edicts 'were frequently ignored, and many merchants wilfully evaded taxation and freely used relay stations'. CAUTION: FP3's definition reads 'confers legal-status or access arbitrage for its PRINCIPALS', and here the arbitrage accrues to the agent. The characteristic is written around a form whose beneficiaries are its members; a capital-labour contract has no such symmetry.

Endicott-West's cell. Official oversight and taxation are described as a LATER reform ('Some Mongol leaders made administrative and economic reforms, starting in the second half of the thirteenth century'), so registration is not evidence about the early regime. Left .NR rather than 0 — nobody asks whether the early ortoq was registered.
Unchanged from the equity regime: the Mongol side supplies capital and the ortoq supplies enterprise. What changes is the legal character of the capital.

REVERSED FROM ortoq_equity, AND THIS IS THE FINDING. 'Consequently, ortoqs were completely liable for the loans they took, which extended beyond partnership capital to their private properties, meaning that ortoq borrowers had to pay back the principal and interest as required.' The agent now bears the principal's capital loss. Same value as isqa, reached from the opposite starting point.
Borrower and lender, with a guarantor standing outside the contract rather than as a third principal. Medium for the same reasons as ortoq_equity CF3.

Liability reaches private property and beyond it to the person: 'Properties could be seized, and if they were insufficient to clear the debt, defaulters and their families were taken into slavery' (Rashid al-Din 1998, 726). Coded several rather than joint because the guarantor's obligation is a separate undertaking — 'the guarantor unconditionally guaranteed the full payment of the debt' — not co-liability among partners. Same value as isqa.
The agent remains bound to the venture's outcome; what changes is the direction. See LR6.

Under loan financing the return to the Mongol side is a fixed claim, not a proportional share — the Yuan government lent to ortoqs at 0.8 per cent a month in the early years of Qubilai's reign (Allsen 1989, 119). Medium because Enkhbold does not say the two arrangements were mutually exclusive in practice and both are attested in the Yuan period; the value records the loan contract's own logic.
Observed absence; nothing is mutualised across a membership.
Inapplicable where LR4 is 0. Propagated .NA.

The call option is gone: the ortoq keeps the residual above the interest and bears the whole downside, to the point of enslavement. Same value as isqa. The pair ortoq_equity/ortoq_loan therefore separates on LR6 within a single institution — the first time the census records a form traversing the agent-loss-exposure axis rather than sitting at a point on it.

Reversed from ortoq_equity. The shielded party in the equity regime was the Mongol principal; under loan financing the exposed party is the ortoq, whose private property and family are reachable. Note the asymmetry this exposes in AP3 itself: the characteristic asks whether members' personal assets are shielded from entity creditors, but in a bilateral capital-labour contract 'member' has two referents and they move in opposite directions.
Unknown, as for ortoq_equity. Enkhbold's statement that the maximum validity 'is not entirely clear' is not periodised, so it cannot be resolved for the later regime either.
Per-contract accounting; no common fund.
The claim arises from the loan instrument.

Endicott-West's cell. Enkhbold reports through her that punishment for defaulting ortoqs was 'confirmed in writing in 1295' (Endicott-West 1989, 149) and that reforms made ortoqs 'subject to official oversight and liable to taxation' — but oversight is not authorisation, and the source that would settle what constituted an ortoq in law has not been read.

Trade and money-lending, the latter at compounded rates the sources put at 100 per cent a year — 'one ding of capital will be 1,024 ding in ten years' (Peng Daya). The Yuan attempt to mandate 3 per cent failed; Dunhuang contracts show 200-300 per cent on some private loans.

Still a wrapper, and now a contested one: the reforms restricting relay-station use and imposing taxation are evidence that the privilege was worth restricting. Same caution as ortoq_equity FP3 about the definition's 'principals'.

THE CELL MOST LIKELY TO SEPARATE THE TWO REGIMES ONCE ENDICOTT-WEST IS READ. Enkhbold reports oversight, taxation and a written penal rule of 1295, which points toward registration, but he is reporting her at second hand and the coding may not exceed that. Do not fill this from Enkhbold.
